messages.author: 2d0051589145ae32
messages.subject: Bootstrap with ordinal endogenous variables
parts:
Hello everyone,

If all of my model's endogenous variables are ordinal variables and my model is also the saturated model, can I use bootstrap to find the effect composition of variables (direct, indirect, and total effects)?

If yes, what does the syntax look like?

Thank you in advance,
Para

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Bootstrap with ordinal endogenous variables
parts: If all of my model's endogenous variables are ordinal variables and my model is also the saturated model, can I use bootstrap to find the effect composition of variables (direct, indirect, and total effects)?
Yes.
If yes, what does the syntax look like?

That depends on your model.  Try writing your syntax, then sharing it with a question if it does not work.  Here is a tutorial on mediation with a simple example:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

And this tutorial page shows how to declare endogenous variables as ordinal:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear Professor Jorgensen,

Thank you very much for the tutorial.
I had followed the tutorial and have two more questions.
The default (Delta) method worked for finding indirect and total effects. ฺBelow is the syntax and result output.

> sem2 <- 'attitude ~ a_t*age + education + involvement + persuasion + netincome + tenure + activity + pastwork + marketing + weather + opportunity + networking + government 
+          happiness ~ a_h*age + education + involvement + persuasion + netincome + tenure + activity + pastwork + marketing + weather + opportunity + networking + government
+          objective ~ a_o*age + education + involvement + persuasion + netincome + tenure + activity + pastwork + marketing + weather + opportunity + networking + government 
+          probability ~ a_p*age + education + involvement + persuasion + netincome + tenure + activity + pastwork + marketing + weather + opportunity + networking + government
+          objective ~ t_o*attitude
+          happiness ~ t_h*attitude + o_h*objective
+          probability ~ t_p*attitude + h_p*happiness + o_p*objective
+          dir := a_p
+          ind_t1 := a_t*t_p
+          ind_t2 := a_t*t_h*h_p
+          ind_t3 := a_t*t_o*o_p
+          ind_t4 := a_t*t_o*o_h*h_p
+          ind_h := a_h*h_p 
+          ind_o1 := a_o*o_p
+          ind_o2 := a_o*o_h*h_p
+          tot_ind := a_t*t_p + a_t*t_h*h_p + a_t*t_o*o_p + a_t*t_o*o_h*h_p + a_h*h_p + a_o*o_p + a_o*o_h*h_p          
+          tot := a_t*t_p + a_t*t_h*h_p + a_t*t_o*o_p + a_t*t_o*o_h*h_p + a_h*h_p + a_o*o_p + a_o*o_h*h_p + a_p'

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrap with ordinal endogenous variables
parts: the Bootstrap method did not work

You can try fitting your model without bootstrapping, then passing your model to the bootstrapLavaan() function to just get the bootstrap distributions you need (instead of for all parameters).  

Or you could use the semTools::monteCarloMed() function, which is much less computationally intensive and shares most of the benefits of bootstrapping.
can I use the results (in the defined parameters part of the result output) from the Delta method instead of  the Bootstrap method?

The delta method is an asymptotic method.  I'm not sure your N is sufficiently larger than the number of parameters you are estimating for the asymptotic properties to kick in, but I also doubt your N is so small that the Type I error rates would be substantially inflated.  I would compare the delta-method CIs to Monte Carlo CIs.  If they lead to any different conclusions, then the Monte Carlo CIs are more trustworthy.

if some indirect effects obtained from the Delta method are insignificant, can I still directly calculate by hand and interpret indirect and total effects from each significant path coefficient in the regressions part of the result output?

Why would you need to do that?  If the user-defined parameters at the bottom of your summary() output are insignificant, it implies your data are consistent with the null hypothesis.  But calculating the indirect effects by hand would not be any different than the calculated estimates at the bottom of your summary() output.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Para,

Tackling the standard question: When using asymmetric confidence
intervals from the bootstrap or monteCarloMed, the standard error is
not part of the computation. The use of the standard error implies the
assumption that the sampling distribution (and therefore the CI) is
symmetric, and can cause more confusion than it resolves when reported
in tandem.

The point estimates involved in computing the standardized
coefficients are generally going to be the best estimated by your
ML(R) or WLSMV run, so you can use those from that run, even if you're
using asymmetric CIs for other purposes, since standardizd should
usually not be used for hypothesis evaluation.

Pat

Para,

Tackling the standard question: When using asymmetric confidence
intervals from the bootstrap or monteCarloMed, the standard error is
not part of the computation. The use of the standard error implies the
assumption that the sampling distribution (and therefore the CI) is
symmetric, and can cause more confusion than it resolves when reported
in tandem.

The point estimates involved in computing the standardized
coefficients are generally going to be the best estimated by your
ML(R) or WLSMV run, so you can use those from that run, even if you're
using asymmetric CIs for other purposes, since standardizd should
usually not be used for hypothesis evaluation.

Pat

> On Sunday, November 29, 2020 at 2:54:36 AM UTC+7 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>>>
>>> the Bootstrap method did not work
>>
>>
>> You can try fitting your model without bootstrapping, then passing your model to the bootstrapLavaan() function to just get the bootstrap distributions you need (instead of for all parameters).
>>
>> Or you could use the semTools::monteCarloMed() function, which is much less computationally intensive and shares most of the benefits of bootstrapping.
>>
>>>
>>> can I use the results (in the defined parameters part of the result output) from the Delta method instead of the Bootstrap method?
>>
>>
>> The delta method is an asymptotic method. I'm not sure your N is sufficiently larger than the number of parameters you are estimating for the asymptotic properties to kick in, but I also doubt your N is so small that the Type I error rates would be substantially inflated. I would compare the delta-method CIs to Monte Carlo CIs. If they lead to any different conclusions, then the Monte Carlo CIs are more trustworthy.
>>
>>> if some indirect effects obtained from the Delta method are insignificant, can I still directly calculate by hand and interpret indirect and total effects from each significant path coefficient in the regressions part of the result output?
>>
>>
>> Why would you need to do that? If the user-defined parameters at the bottom of your summary() output are insignificant, it implies your data are consistent with the null hypothesis. But calculating the indirect effects by hand would not be any different than the calculated estimates at the bottom of your summary() output.
>>

When you fit your model, you can set conditional.x=FALSE.  It is TRUE by default because it is less of a computational burden, but it would not change your results to set it FALSE so that you can use bootstrapLavaan()
